101.solution: A plane parallel to the XY-plane has the form \(z = k\) (its normal is along the Z-axis). Since it passes through \(A(7,8,6)\), we get \(z = 6\).

102.solution: Seat the 6 boys around the round table first: \((6-1)! = 5! = 120\) ways. This creates 6 gaps between consecutive boys. Place the 5 girls in these 6 gaps so that no two girls are together: \(^{6}P_{5} = 720\) ways. Total \(= 120 \times 720 = 86400\).

103.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
103.solution: Treat each bracket as a scalar triple product, linear in each slot. The left side \([2\bar p - 3\bar r,\ \bar q,\ \bar s] + [3\bar p + 2\bar q,\ \bar r,\ \bar s]\) expands. The first term \(= 2[\bar p,\bar q,\bar s] - 3[\bar r,\bar q,\bar s]\). The second \(= 3[\bar p,\bar r,\bar s] + 2[\bar q,\bar r,\bar s]\). Using \([\bar r,\bar q,\bar s] = -[\bar q,\bar r,\bar s]\), the \(-3[\bar r,\bar q,\bar s]\) becomes \(+3[\bar q,\bar r,\bar s]\). Collecting: \(3[\bar p,\bar r,\bar s] + 5[\bar q,\bar r,\bar s] + 2[\bar p,\bar q,\bar s]\). Comparing with \(m[\bar p,\bar r,\bar s] + n[\bar q,\bar r,\bar s] + t[\bar p,\bar q,\bar s]\) gives \(m=3,\ n=5,\ t=2\).
103.note: Stem prints '2p-3r' for the first matrix; akSolution treats first entry as 2p (text shows p-3r, likely OCR). The comparison m,n,t = 3,5,2 matches option D regardless.

104.subtopic: Distance, Foot of Perpendicular, Projection, and Mirror Image
104.solution: Line: \((4,6,-2) + \lambda(-1,2,3)\), so \(Q = (4-\lambda,\ 6+2\lambda,\ -2+3\lambda)\). With \(P(-3,2,3)\), \(\overline{PQ}\) has d.r.s \((7-\lambda,\ 4+2\lambda,\ -5+3\lambda)\). Foot: \(\overline{PQ}\perp\) line, so \(-1(7-\lambda)+2(4+2\lambda)+3(-5+3\lambda)=0 \Rightarrow -7+\lambda+8+4\lambda-15+9\lambda=0 \Rightarrow 14\lambda=14 \Rightarrow \lambda=1\). Then \(Q=(3,8,1)\) and \(PQ=\sqrt{6^2+6^2+(-2)^2}=\sqrt{76}=2\sqrt{19}\).

105.solution: Required plane normal \((a,b,c)\) is perpendicular to the normals of both given planes, so it is along \((2,-2,1)\times(1,-1,2)\). Compute: \(\hat i(-2\cdot2-1\cdot(-1)) - \hat j(2\cdot2-1\cdot1) + \hat k(2\cdot(-1)-(-2)\cdot1) = \hat i(-3) - \hat j(3) + \hat k(0) = (-3,-3,0)\), i.e. direction \((1,1,0)\). Plane through \((1,-2,1)\): \(1(x-1)+1(y+2)=0 \Rightarrow x+y+1=0\). Distance of \((1,2,2)\): \(\left|\dfrac{1+2+1}{\sqrt{2}}\right| = \dfrac{4}{\sqrt2} = 2\sqrt2\).

106.subtopic: Section Formula, Concurrency, Foot of Perpendicular, and Distance
106.solution: The rectangle has vertices at the intersections of \(x=8,x=10\) with \(y=11,y=12\): \((8,11),(10,11),(10,12),(8,12)\). The diagonals intersect at the centre, which is the average of opposite corners: \(\left(\dfrac{8+10}{2},\dfrac{11+12}{2}\right) = \left(9,\dfrac{23}{2}\right)\).

107.subtopic: Basic Probability — Events, Conditional, and Complement
107.solution: Odd tickets: 5 (1,3,5,7,9); even: 4 (2,4,6,8). Drawn one at a time without replacement. \(P(\text{O,E,O}) = \dfrac{5}{9}\cdot\dfrac{4}{8}\cdot\dfrac{4}{7} = \dfrac{80}{504}\). \(P(\text{E,O,E}) = \dfrac{4}{9}\cdot\dfrac{5}{8}\cdot\dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{60}{504}\). Sum \(= \dfrac{140}{504} = \dfrac{5}{18}\).

109.subtopic: Negation, Equivalence, Tautology, and Switch Circuits
109.solution: \([(p\to q)\wedge \sim q]\) is true only when \(p\to q\) is true and \(q\) is false, which forces \(p\) false (and \(q\) false). For the conditional \([(p\to q)\wedge \sim q]\to r\) to be a tautology, \(r\) must be true whenever the antecedent is true, i.e. whenever \(q\) is false. So \(r\) must be true exactly when \(\sim q\) is true; \(r\equiv \sim q\) guarantees this.

110.subtopic: Trig Identities, Compound Angle, and Equations
110.solution: Let \(\theta=\dfrac{\alpha+\beta}{2},\ \phi=\dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\), so \(\alpha=\theta+\phi,\ \beta=\theta-\phi\). Then \(3\sin\alpha=5\sin\beta\) gives \(3\sin(\theta+\phi)=5\sin(\theta-\phi)\). Expanding: \(3(\sin\theta\cos\phi+\cos\theta\sin\phi)=5(\sin\theta\cos\phi-\cos\theta\sin\phi)\). So \(8\cos\theta\sin\phi=2\sin\theta\cos\phi \Rightarrow \dfrac{\tan\theta}{\tan\phi}=4\). Hence \(\dfrac{\tan\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}}{\tan\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}}=4\).
110.note: Stem prints a '+' between the two tan terms but the worked relation (and options) require the RATIO = 4; this is a known OCR sign issue. Answer 4 matches D either way.

111.solution: Let \(t=e^x\), \(dt=e^x\,dx=t\,dx\). Then \(I=\int\dfrac{dt}{t(2t^2+3t+1)}=\int\dfrac{dt}{t(2t+1)(t+1)}\). Partial fractions: \(\dfrac{1}{t(2t+1)(t+1)}=\dfrac{1}{t}-\dfrac{4}{2t+1}+\dfrac{1}{t+1}\). Integrating: \(\ln t - 2\ln|2t+1| + \ln|t+1| = x + \ln(e^x+1) - 2\ln(2e^x+1) + c\).

113.solution: Split by the greatest-integer value: \([x]=1\) on \((1,2)\), \(=2\) on \((2,3)\), \(=3\) on \((3,4)\). So \(\int_1^4 \log[x]\,dx = \int_1^2 \log1\,dx + \int_2^3 \log2\,dx + \int_3^4 \log3\,dx = 0 + \log2 + \log3 = \log6\).

114.subtopic: Order, Degree, Formation of ODE, and Verification of Solutions
114.solution: Tangent to \(x^2=4y\) (here \(4a=4\), so \(a=1\)) in slope form: \(x=my+\dfrac{1}{m}\), i.e. \(mx=m^2y+1\). Replace \(m=\dfrac{dy}{dx}\): \(x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 y + 1\). This is order 1, degree 2.

115.subtopic: Probability Distribution — Constants, Expectation, and Variance
115.solution: Probabilities are \(2k,k,2k,4k,k\) for \(X=0,1,2,3,4\). Sum \(=10k=1\Rightarrow k=\dfrac{1}{10}\). \(a=P(X<3)=2k+k+2k=5k=\dfrac{1}{2}\). \(b=P(2\le X<4)=P(2)+P(3)=2k+4k=6k=\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}\). Since \(\dfrac{1}{2}<\dfrac{3}{5}\), we have \(a<b\).

116.subtopic: Probability Distribution — Constants, Expectation, and Variance
116.solution: Find \(k\) from \(\int_0^\infty \dfrac{k}{x^2+1}\,dx=1 \Rightarrow k[\tan^{-1}x]_0^\infty = k\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=1 \Rightarrow k=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\). The c.d.f. is \(F(x)=\int_0^x \dfrac{2/\pi}{t^2+1}\,dt = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\tan^{-1}x\) for \(x>0\).

117.solution: Separate: \(\dfrac{dy}{1+y} = \dfrac{-\cos x}{2+\sin x}\,dx\). Integrate: \(\ln(1+y) = -\ln(2+\sin x) + \ln c\), so \((1+y)(2+\sin x)=c\). With \(y(0)=2\): \((3)(2)=c=6\). Then \(y\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)+1 = \dfrac{6}{2+1}=2 \Rightarrow y=1\).

118.solution: \(\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{x}{100}P \Rightarrow \ln P = \dfrac{x}{100}t + c\). The amount doubles in 10 years: \(\ln\dfrac{200}{100}=\dfrac{x}{100}\cdot10\), so \(\dfrac{x}{10}=\ln2=0.6931 \Rightarrow x=6.931\approx 6.93\%\).

119.subtopic: Binomial Distribution — Mean, Variance, and Parameter Estimation
119.solution: \(B(33,p)\): \(3P(X=0)=P(X=1)\) gives \(3q^{33}=33pq^{32}\Rightarrow 3q=33p\Rightarrow q=11p\). With \(p+q=1\): \(12p=1\Rightarrow p=\dfrac{1}{12},\ q=\dfrac{11}{12}\). Variance \(=npq=33\cdot\dfrac{1}{12}\cdot\dfrac{11}{12}=\dfrac{363}{144}=\dfrac{121}{48}\).

120.subtopic: Two Circles — Tangency, Common Tangents, and Relative Position
120.solution: Circle 1: \(x^2+y^2-6x=0\), centre \(C_1(3,0)\), \(r_1=3\). Circle 2: \(x^2+y^2+6x+2y+1=0\), centre \(C_2(-3,-1)\), \(r_2=\sqrt{9+1-1}=3\). \(C_1C_2=\sqrt{36+1}=\sqrt{37}\approx6.08\). Since \(C_1C_2 > r_1+r_2=6\), the circles are external (no overlap), so 4 common tangents exist.

121.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Identities, Equations, Principal Values, and Sums
121.solution: The general term \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2^{n-1}}{1+2^{2n-1}} = \tan^{-1}\dfrac{2^n-2^{n-1}}{1+2^n\cdot2^{n-1}} = \tan^{-1}2^n - \tan^{-1}2^{n-1}\). This telescopes: partial sum \(= \tan^{-1}2^n - \tan^{-1}1\). As \(n\to\infty\): \(\tan^{-1}(\infty) - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{4} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

122.solution: Sides \(5x,12x,13x\) form a right triangle (since \(5^2+12^2=13^2\)), right-angled at the vertex opposite \(13x\). Area \(=\dfrac{1}{2}(5x)(12x)=30x^2=270 \Rightarrow x^2=9 \Rightarrow x=3\). Sides: \(15,36,39\).

123.subtopic: Inverse Trigonometric Functions — Identities, Equations, Principal Values, and Sums

124.solution: Rewrite: \(\int_1^e e^x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}+\log x\right)dx\). This is of the form \(\int e^x[f(x)+f'(x)]dx\) with \(f(x)=\log x,\ f'(x)=\dfrac{1}{x}\), giving \([e^x\log x]_1^e = e^e\cdot1 - e^1\cdot0 = e^e\).

125.subtopic: Area Bounded by Curves, Axes, and Lines

126.solution: \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=\dfrac{1}{x}\). Integrate: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\log x + c\). With \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0\) at \(x=1\): \(c=0\). Integrate again: \(y=\int\log x\,dx = x\log x - x + k\). With \(x=y=1\): \(1=0-1+k\Rightarrow k=2\). So \(y=x\log x - x + 2\).

127.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
127.solution: Volume of tetrahedron \(=\dfrac{1}{6}|[\bar a,\bar b,\bar c]| = 12\), so \([\bar a,\bar b,\bar c]=\bar a\cdot(\bar b\times\bar c)=72\). Scalar projection of \(\bar a\) on \(\bar b\times\bar c\) is \(\dfrac{\bar a\cdot(\bar b\times\bar c)}{|\bar b\times\bar c|}=4\). Thus \(|\bar b\times\bar c|=\dfrac{72}{4}=18\).

128.subtopic: Distance, Foot of Perpendicular, Projection, and Mirror Image
128.solution: Squared distances from the axes: from X-axis \(=y^2+z^2\), from Y-axis \(=x^2+z^2\), from Z-axis \(=x^2+y^2\). Their sum \(=2(x^2+y^2+z^2)=242\), so \(x^2+y^2+z^2=121\). Distance from origin \(=\sqrt{121}=11\).

129.subtopic: Scalar Triple Product, Coplanarity, and Volume
129.solution: With \(A(2-x,2,2),B(2,2-y,2),C(2,2,2-z),D(1,1,1)\): \(\overline{AB}=(x,-y,0)\), \(\overline{AC}=(x,0,-z)\), \(\overline{AD}=(x-1,-1,-1)\). Coplanar \(\Rightarrow \begin{vmatrix} x&-y&0\\ x&0&-z\\ x-1&-1&-1\end{vmatrix}=0\). Expanding: \(x(0\cdot(-1)-(-z)(-1)) - (-y)(x(-1)-(-z)(x-1)) + 0 = x(-z) + y(-x + z(x-1)) = -xz - xy + xyz - yz = 0\). Dividing by \(xyz\): \(\dfrac{1}{y}+\dfrac{1}{z}+\dfrac{1}{x}-1=0\), i.e. \(\dfrac{1}{x}+\dfrac{1}{y}+\dfrac{1}{z}=1\).

130.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
130.solution: Line 1 \(\dfrac{3-x}{2}=\dfrac{5y-2}{3\lambda+1}=5-z\): rewrite as \(\dfrac{x-3}{-2}=\dfrac{y-2/5}{(3\lambda+1)/5}=\dfrac{z-5}{-1}\), d.r.s \(\left(-2,\dfrac{3\lambda+1}{5},-1\right)\). Line 2 \(\dfrac{x+2}{-1}=\dfrac{1-3y}{7}=\dfrac{4-z}{2\mu}\): \(\dfrac{x+2}{-1}=\dfrac{y-1/3}{-7/3}=\dfrac{z-4}{-2\mu}\), d.r.s \(\left(-1,-\dfrac{7}{3},-2\mu\right)\). Perpendicular: \((-2)(-1)+\dfrac{3\lambda+1}{5}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right)+(-1)(-2\mu)=0\). So \(2 - \dfrac{7(3\lambda+1)}{15} + 2\mu = 0\). Multiply by 15: \(30 - 21\lambda - 7 + 30\mu = 0 \Rightarrow 21\lambda - 30\mu = 23 \Rightarrow 7\lambda - 10\mu = \dfrac{23}{3}\).
130.note: Flawed: my derivation and the AK's own worked solution both give 7*lambda - 10*mu = 23/3, which is NOT among the printed options (143, 143/3, 137, 137/5). Keyed D contradicts the AK algebra. Likely an options/key transcription error in the LWS reproduction. Kept PRIVATE.

131.subtopic: Angles — Line, Plane, and Direction Conditions
131.solution: Line d.r.s \((1,2,2)\); plane normal \((2,-1,\sqrt\lambda)\). \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{|1\cdot2+2\cdot(-1)+2\sqrt\lambda|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}\,\sqrt{4+1+\lambda}} = \dfrac{2\sqrt\lambda}{3\sqrt{5+\lambda}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). So \(2\sqrt\lambda=\sqrt{5+\lambda}\Rightarrow 4\lambda=5+\lambda\Rightarrow \lambda=\dfrac{5}{3}\). Then \(\lambda+1=\dfrac{8}{3}\).

132.solution: The feasible region must satisfy: \(2x+3y\ge12\) (non-origin side of that line), \(-x+y\le3\) (origin side), \(x\le4\) (left of \(x=4\)), and \(y\ge3\) (above \(y=3\)). Testing \((3,4)\): \(2(3)+3(4)=18\ge12\) ✓, \(-3+4=1\le3\) ✓, \(3\le4\) ✓, \(4\ge3\) ✓. From the figure this point lies in region \(S_1\) (just above \(y=3\), right of the \(2x+3y=12\) line, left of \(x=4\), below \(-x+y=3\)). Hence the region is \(S_1\).
132.note: Figure read: S1 is the small region above y=3 bounded by 2x+3y=12 (left), x=4 (right), -x+y=3 (top). Matches all constraints.

134.solution: Each factor \(\cos(2k-1)x+i\sin(2k-1)x = e^{i(2k-1)x}\). The product over \(k=1\) to \(n\) gives \(e^{i(1+3+\cdots+(2n-1))x} = e^{i n^2 x}\) (sum of first \(n\) odd numbers \(=n^2\)). So \(f(x)=e^{in^2x}\), \(f'(x)=in^2 e^{in^2x}\), \(f''(x)=(in^2)^2 e^{in^2x} = -n^4 e^{in^2x} = -n^4 f(x)\).

136.subtopic: Conic Properties — Eccentricity, Orthogonality, and Intersection
136.solution: B is an end of the minor axis \((0,b)\); foci \(S(ae,0),S'(-ae,0)\). \(\angle SBS'=90^\circ\) means \(\overline{BS}\perp\overline{BS'}\). By symmetry, each of \(\angle SBO\) is \(45^\circ\), so \(b=ae\) (the legs OB and OS are equal). Then \(b^2=a^2e^2\) and \(b^2=a^2(1-e^2)\) give \(a^2e^2=a^2(1-e^2)\Rightarrow 2e^2=1\Rightarrow e=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\).

142.solution: \(I=\int\dfrac{\sin2x}{(a+b\cos x)^2}dx=\int\dfrac{2\sin x\cos x}{(a+b\cos x)^2}dx\). Let \(t=a+b\cos x\), \(\cos x=\dfrac{t-a}{b}\), \(dt=-b\sin x\,dx\), so \(\sin x\,dx=-\dfrac{dt}{b}\). Then \(I=\int\dfrac{2\cdot\frac{t-a}{b}}{t^2}\cdot\left(-\dfrac{dt}{b}\right)=-\dfrac{2}{b^2}\int\dfrac{t-a}{t^2}dt = -\dfrac{2}{b^2}\left[\ln|t|+\dfrac{a}{t}\right]+c = -\dfrac{2}{b^2}\left[\log(a+b\cos x)+\dfrac{a}{a+b\cos x}\right]+c\).

143.subtopic: Combined Equation and Condition for Pair of Lines
143.solution: For \(ax^2+2hxy+by^2=0\): \(m_1+m_2=-\dfrac{2h}{b},\ m_1m_2=\dfrac{a}{b}\). Then \(\dfrac{(m_1+m_2)^2}{m_1m_2}=\dfrac{4h^2/b^2}{a/b}=\dfrac{4h^2}{ab}\). Given \(6h^2=25ab\Rightarrow \dfrac{h^2}{ab}=\dfrac{25}{6}\), so \(\dfrac{(m_1+m_2)^2}{m_1m_2}=\dfrac{4\cdot25}{6}=\dfrac{50}{3}\). Let \(m_1=km_2\): \(\dfrac{(k+1)^2}{k}=\dfrac{50}{3}\Rightarrow 3k^2+6k+3=50k\Rightarrow 3k^2-44k+3=0\). Hmm, this gives non-integer ratios; with the AK reading \(16h^2=25ab\) the ratio is \(\dfrac{4\cdot25/16}{1}=\dfrac{(k+1)^2}{k}\Rightarrow\dfrac{25}{4}=\dfrac{(k+1)^2}{k}\Rightarrow 4k^2-17k+4=0\Rightarrow k=4\) or \(1/4\). So \(m_1=4m_2\).

144.solution: Conjugate of \(-7+24i\) is \(-7-24i\), with modulus \(\sqrt{49+576}=\sqrt{625}=25\). The modulus of a square root is \(\sqrt{|z|}=\sqrt{25}=5\).

146.subtopic: Continuity at a Point — Finding Parameters
146.solution: Continuity at 0 requires both one-sided limits equal \(f(0)=\dfrac{2}{\log2}\). Left: \(\lim_{x\to0^-}\dfrac{3\sin x+5\tan x}{a^x-1}=\dfrac{3+5}{\log a}=\dfrac{8}{\log a}\). Setting \(\dfrac{8}{\log a}=\dfrac{2}{\log2}\Rightarrow\log a=4\log2\Rightarrow a=16\). Right: \(\lim_{x\to0^+}\dfrac{8x+2x\cos x}{b^x-1}=\dfrac{8+2}{\log b}=\dfrac{10}{\log b}=\dfrac{2}{\log2}\Rightarrow\log b=5\log2\Rightarrow b=32\). So \(a=16,b=32\).

147.solution: Smallest angle is opposite the smallest side. Sides: \(a=6+\sqrt{12}=6+2\sqrt3,\ b=\sqrt{48}=4\sqrt3,\ c=\sqrt{24}=2\sqrt6\). Smallest side is \(c=2\sqrt6\approx4.9\). \(\cos C=\dfrac{a^2+b^2-c^2}{2ab}\). \(a^2=48+24\sqrt3,\ b^2=48,\ c^2=24\). Numerator \(=48+24\sqrt3+48-24=72+24\sqrt3=24(3+\sqrt3)\). Denominator \(=2(6+2\sqrt3)(4\sqrt3)=8\sqrt3(6+2\sqrt3)=16\sqrt3(3+\sqrt3)\). So \(\cos C=\dfrac{24(3+\sqrt3)}{16\sqrt3(3+\sqrt3)}=\dfrac{24}{16\sqrt3}=\dfrac{3}{2\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\). Hence \(C=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

148.solution: \(p\): \(10n-3\) prime when \(n\) not divisible by 3 — fails (e.g. \(n=8\): \(77=7\times11\)), so \(p\) is False. \(q\): \(\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{-2}{\sqrt3}\right)^2+\left(\frac{-1}{\sqrt3}\right)^2=\frac{4+4+1}{3}=3\neq1\), so these are NOT direction cosines; \(q\) is False. \(r\): \(\sin x\) increasing on \([-\pi/2,\pi/2]\) since \(\cos x\ge0\) there; \(r\) is True. Now \((\sim p\vee q)\wedge r=(T\vee F)\wedge T=T\). Option C is true.

149.solution: The sum \(a_{21}A_{21}+a_{22}A_{22}+a_{23}A_{23}\) is the cofactor expansion of \(\det(A)\) along row 2, which equals \(\det(A)\). For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&\sin\theta&0\\-\sin\theta&\cos\theta&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}\), \(\det A=1\cdot(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=1\). So the value is 1.

150.solution: Let \(\dfrac{b+c}{11}=\dfrac{c+a}{12}=\dfrac{a+b}{13}=k\). Adding: \(2(a+b+c)=36k\Rightarrow a+b+c=18k\). Then \(a=18k-11k=7k,\ b=18k-12k=6k,\ c=18k-13k=5k\). Using the cosine rule: \(\cos A=\dfrac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}=\dfrac{36+25-49}{60}=\dfrac{12}{60}=\dfrac15\); \(\cos B=\dfrac{49+25-36}{70}=\dfrac{38}{70}=\dfrac{19}{35}\); \(\cos C=\dfrac{49+36-25}{84}=\dfrac{60}{84}=\dfrac57\). Ratio \(\dfrac15:\dfrac{19}{35}:\dfrac57\); multiply by 35: \(7:19:25\).
